questions_and_answers.question_text: What two additional meanings does yào have here?
How is bàn- used when it PRECEDES a counter?
How is bàn translated when it FOLLOWS a counter?
What is the literal meaning of xiǎoshí?
Write the Chinese for "half an hour" and "one and a half hours."
Write the Chinese for "It probably takes four and a half hours."

answers.answer_text: Dàgài yào zǒu sìge bàn xiǎoshí.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Give the Chinese for "two and a half dollars" and "three and a half days."
How was a day and night formerly divided?

answers.answer_text: Into twelve 2-hour periods, each divided into two xiǎoshí.

questions_and_answers.question_text: Write the Chinese for "half a year."

articles.text:
3. A: Zuò huǒchē yào zǒu duōshao     How long does it take to go by
      shíhou?                         train?
   B: Dàgài yào zǒu sìge bàn         It probably takes four and a half
      xiǎoshí.                        hours.

4. C: Yào zǒu bànge xiǎoshí.         It takes half an hour.

Notes on Nos. 3-4

The auxiliary verb yào, "to want," is sometimes used as "to need to," "to have to." Yào may also be used as a main verb meaning "to take (a certain amount of time)."

Bàn-, "a half (of)," is used like a number--before a counter or before a noun which does not require a counter.

bànge xiǎoshí                    half an hour
bànnián                          half a year
bànge píngguǒ                    half an apple

Sìge bàn: When bàn FOLLOWS a counter or a noun not requiring a counter, the word is translated as "and a half."

liǎngkuài bàn                    two and a half dollars
sāntian bàn                      three and a half days
yíge bàn xiǎoshí                 one and a half hours

Xiǎoshí: Formerly, the Chinese considered that one day and night (24 hours) was divided into twelve 2-hour periods of time. Each of these time periods was divided into two xiǎoshí, "small hours," when telling time by the Western 24-hour system gained popularity throughout the world.
